--- title: "Data Model & Dtypes" subtitle: "≈ tibble · atomic vectors · vctrs coercion" jupyter: python3 --- Before expressions, the data they run on. A Polars `DataFrame` is a tibble with a larger and stricter type system. This chapter covers the three containers, how a column sits in memory, the dtype catalogue mapped to R's types, and the coercion rules: Polars refuses to coerce in places where R would, and silently wraps integers in places where R would warn. ## In tidyverse {#sec-dm-tidyverse} ```r library(palmerpenguins) typeof(penguins$body_mass_g) # "integer": a 32-bit atomic vector attributes(penguins$species) # $levels, $class "factor": an integer + attributes unclass(as.Date("2025-01-01")) # 20089: a Date is a number + a class c(1L, 2.5) # silently becomes double dplyr::bind_rows(tibble(a = 1L), tibble(a = 2.5)) # a becomes double as.integer(c("1", "x")) # 1 NA, with a warning as.integer("3.7") # 3 .Machine$integer.max + 1L # NA, with a warning ``` R's model: a tibble is a named list of equal-length atomic vectors. There are a handful of atomic types, and everything richer (factor, Date, POSIXct) is one of them plus attributes. Coercion is generous: base R and vctrs pick a common type and carry on. Polars has many more types, and it coerces only when you ask it to. ## Mental model {#sec-dm-model} ```text df["x"] / df.get_column("x") df.lazy() Series ◄───────────────────────────── DataFrame ──────────────► LazyFrame ─────────────────────────────► ◄────────────── s.to_frame() lf.collect() one named, typed column equal-length Series, a query plan: ≈ an atomic vector unique names, no no data until collect() row names ≈ tibble ≈ a dbplyr lazy tbl Inside a Series (Apache Arrow layout) ┌──────────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐ │ values │ 3750 │ 3800 │ 3250 │ · │ 3450 │ one contiguous buffer, fixed-width dtype │ validity │ 1 │ 1 │ 1 │ 0 │ 1 │ 1 bit per row: 0 = null └──────────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘ ``` Two consequences: - **Null is a separate bit, not a special value.** In R, `NA_integer_` *is* a value (the smallest 32-bit integer is reserved for it) and `NA_real_` is a NaN with a special payload. In Polars, any dtype can be null, and null and `NaN` are different things (see [Missing Values](../types/missing.qmd)). - **A column is the unit of work.** Selecting, adding or dropping a column never touches the others, which is why returning a new frame from every verb is cheap (@sec-dm-sharing). ## Mechanics {#sec-dm-mechanics} ::: {#95e37209 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import datetime as dt from decimal import Decimal import polars as pl import polars.selectors as cs from pl_notes import datasets penguins_df = datasets.penguins() flights_df = datasets.flights() ``` ::: ### Series, DataFrame, LazyFrame {#sec-dm-containers} Pulling one column out gives a `Series`, the equivalent of `penguins$body_mass_g`: ::: {#625a31e3 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} mass = penguins_df["body_mass_g"] mass.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
shape: (3,)
body_mass_g
i64
3750
3800
3250
``` ::: ::: A `Series` is data, already computed. It supports most expression methods directly, and because it stands alone, `sort()` can't misalign anything: ::: {#f40b1963 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} mass.mean(), mass.null_count(), mass.sort(descending=True, nulls_last=True).head(2).to_list() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (4201.754385964912, 2, [6300, 6050]) ``` ::: ::: Don't confuse it with the expression that names the same column: | R | Polars | What it is | |---|---|---| | `penguins$body_mass_g` | `penguins_df["body_mass_g"]` | a `Series`: data, computed now | | bare `body_mass_g` inside `mutate()` | `pl.col("body_mass_g")` | an `Expr`: a recipe (see [Expressions & Contexts](expressions.qmd)) | : Series vs Expr {.striped} A `Series` can go straight into a context, like `mutate(z = some_vector)`. Its length must match the frame's height: ::: {#609718b6 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} weights = pl.Series("weight", [0.5, 1.0, 2.0] * 114 + [1.0, 1.0]) # 344 values penguins_df.with_columns(weights).select("species", "weight").head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 2)
speciesweight
strf64
"Adelie"0.5
"Adelie"1.0
"Adelie"2.0
``` ::: ::: A `LazyFrame` holds a plan instead of data, but it already knows the output schema, and computing that schema reads no data: ::: {#0c8bceab .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.lazy().with_columns( bill_ratio=pl.col("bill_length_mm") / pl.col("bill_depth_mm") ).collect_schema() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` Schema([('species', String), ('island', String), ('bill_length_mm', Float64), ('bill_depth_mm', Float64), ('flipper_length_mm', Int64), ('body_mass_g', Int64), ('sex', String), ('year', Int64), ('bill_ratio', Float64)]) ``` ::: ::: The [Lazy API](../scale/lazy.qmd) chapter covers the rest. ### Columns are shared, not copied {#sec-dm-sharing} Every verb returns a new `DataFrame`. That would be expensive if each one copied the data, but unchanged columns are shared. To prove it, compare the memory address of the `year` buffer before and after: ::: {#fb27143a .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} def buffer_address(s: pl.Series) -> int: """Address of a Series' values (a NumPy view; raises if a copy is needed).""" return s.to_numpy(allow_copy=False).__array_interface__["data"][0] year_address = buffer_address(penguins_df["year"]) { "with_columns(), year untouched": buffer_address( penguins_df.with_columns(year2=pl.col("year") * 2)["year"] ) == year_address, "select('year')": buffer_address(penguins_df.select("year")["year"]) == year_address, "year recomputed": buffer_address( penguins_df.with_columns(pl.col("year") + 0)["year"] ) == year_address, } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` {'with_columns(), year untouched': True, "select('year')": True, 'year recomputed': False} ``` ::: ::: R has done the same since 3.1.0: `mutate()` makes a *shallow* copy, and `lobstr::ref()` shows the unchanged columns pointing at the same memory. In both languages, the style of never modifying in place and always returning a new frame costs almost nothing. ### The dtype catalogue {#sec-dm-dtypes} | R | Polars dtype | Notes | |---|---|---| | `logical` | `Boolean` | bit-packed: 1 bit per value (R uses 32) | | `integer` | `Int32`, but the **default is `Int64`** | also `Int8`, `Int16`, `Int128`, `UInt8` … `UInt128` | | `double` | `Float64` | also `Float32`, `Float16` | | `bit64::integer64` | `Int64` | built in, no extra package | | — | `Decimal(precision, scale)` | exact base-10 arithmetic (@sec-dm-decimal) | | `character` | `String` | UTF-8; `pl.Utf8` is an old alias | | `raw` | `Binary` | | | `factor` | `Categorical`, `Enum` | `Enum` has a fixed set of levels in a fixed order | | `Date` | `Date` | | | `POSIXct` | `Datetime(time_unit, time_zone)` | microseconds by default | | `difftime` | `Duration(time_unit)` | | | `hms::hms` | `Time` | | | list-column | `List(inner)` | every element shares **one** inner dtype | | — | `Array(inner, shape)` | fixed-length list | | data-frame column | `Struct({name: dtype, ...})` | named fields | | an all-`NA` vector | `Null` | the dtype of a column with no values | : R types → Polars dtypes {.striped} What Python values become: ::: {#ec742d43 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.DataFrame({ "int": [1], "float": [1.5], "str": ["a"], "bool": [True], "none": [None], "date": [dt.date(2025, 1, 1)], "datetime": [dt.datetime(2025, 1, 1, 9)], "timedelta": [dt.timedelta(days=1)], "time": [dt.time(9, 30)], "list": [[1, 2]], "dict": [{"a": 1, "b": "x"}], "decimal": [Decimal("1.10")], }).glimpse() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 1 Columns: 12 $ int 1 $ float 1.5 $ str 'a' $ bool True $ none null $ date 2025-01-01 $ datetime 2025-01-01 09:00:00 $ timedelta 1 day, 0:00:00 $ time 09:30:00 $ list [1, 2] $ dict {'a': 1, 'b': 'x'} $ decimal 1.10 ``` ::: ::: To test a dtype, compare it with a dtype **class** to match any parameters, or with an **instance** to match exactly: ::: {#b8653808 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} time_hour_dtype = flights_df.schema["time_hour"] ( time_hour_dtype == pl.Datetime, # any unit, any zone time_hour_dtype == pl.Datetime("us"), # zone differs → False time_hour_dtype == pl.Datetime("us", "America/New_York"), penguins_df.schema["body_mass_g"].is_integer(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` (True, False, True, True) ``` ::: ::: Choosing columns by dtype (`where(is.numeric)`) is covered in [Selectors](selectors.qmd). ### Logical types on physical types {#sec-dm-physical} R stores a Date as a number with a class attribute. Polars does the same: a *logical* dtype is stored as a *physical* one, and `to_physical()` shows the stored values: ::: {#02920eb6 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.select( pl.col("time_hour").head(1), stored=pl.col("time_hour").head(1).to_physical(), # µs since 1970-01-01 UTC ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
shape: (1, 2)
time_hourstored
datetime[μs, America/New_York]i64
2013-01-01 05:00:00 EST1357034400000000
``` ::: ::: The time zone is part of the dtype, not the stored data. R's POSIXct works the same way: seconds since the epoch plus a `tzone` attribute. `Enum` and `Categorical` work like factors, as small unsigned integer codes plus the levels: ::: {#c78f9ec3 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.select( "species", code=pl.col("species").cast(pl.Enum(["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"])).to_physical(), ).unique(maintain_order=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 2)
speciescode
stru8
"Adelie"0
"Gentoo"2
"Chinstrap"1
``` ::: ::: These codes are 0-based, where `as.integer(factor)` is 1-based. ### Integer widths and literal dtypes {#sec-dm-integers} | dtype | range | dtype | range | |---|---|---|---| | `Int8` | −128 … 127 | `UInt8` | 0 … 255 | | `Int16` | −32,768 … 32,767 | `UInt16` | 0 … 65,535 | | `Int32` | ±2.1 × 10⁹ | `UInt32` | 0 … 4.3 × 10⁹ | | `Int64` | ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ | `UInt64` | 0 … 1.8 × 10¹⁹ | : Integer dtypes {.striped} `read_csv()` and Python integers both default to `Int64`, twice the width of R's integer. Smaller widths save memory (@sec-dm-recipes) at the price of overflow risk (@sec-dm-gotchas). When an expression combines two dtypes, Polars computes a **supertype**, much like `vctrs::vec_ptype2()`. A Python literal is more flexible: it takes the column's dtype and widens it only if the value doesn't fit: ::: {#b16b9520 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} narrow_df = pl.DataFrame({ "x_i8": pl.Series([1, 2], dtype=pl.Int8), "x_f32": pl.Series([1.0, 2.0], dtype=pl.Float32), }) narrow_df.select( lit_alone=pl.lit(1), # Int32 plus_1=pl.col("x_i8") + 1, # stays Int8 plus_1000=pl.col("x_i8") + 1000, # 1000 doesn't fit in Int8 → Int16 times_2_5=pl.col("x_f32") * 2.5, # stays Float32 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 4)
lit_aloneplus_1plus_1000times_2_5
i32i8i16f32
1210012.5
1310025.0
``` ::: ::: | Left | Right | Result | |---|---|---| | `Int32` | `Int64` | `Int64` | | `Int64` | `Float32` | `Float64` | | `UInt64` | `Int64` | `Int128` | | `Int8` | literal `1000` | `Int16` | : Supertypes of column-vs-column arithmetic (verified on Polars 2.0) {.striped} ### Casting is strict {#sec-dm-casting} `cast()` fails if **any** value can't be converted, and the error lists the values that failed: ::: {#7f4ba1e0 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.Series(["1", "2", "x"]).cast(pl.Int64) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
InvalidOperationError: conversion from `str` to `i64` failed in column '' for 1 out of 3 values: ["x"]
``` ::: ::: ::: `strict=False` turns those values into null. That is what R's `as.integer()` does, but without the warning: ::: {#2be14474 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.Series(["1", "2", "x"]).cast(pl.Int64, strict=False).to_list() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` [1, 2, None] ``` ::: ::: | Conversion | R | Polars `cast()` | `strict=False` | |---|---|---|---| | `"x"` → integer | `NA` + warning | error | null | | `"3.7"` → integer | `3` | error (cast to `Float64` first) | null | | `3.7` → integer | `3` | `3` (truncates toward zero) | `3` | | `NaN` → integer | `NA` | error | null | | `300` → `Int8` | (no `Int8`) | error | null; `wrap_numerical=True` gives `44` | | `"true"` → logical | `TRUE` | not supported: use `pl.col("x") == "true"` | — | | `1.0` → string | `"1"` | `"1.0"` | — | : Casting rules compared {.striped} To cast a whole frame, pass a `{column: dtype}` mapping. Selectors work as keys too: ::: {#861baafb .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.cast({"year": pl.Int16, cs.float(): pl.Float32}).schema ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` Schema([('species', String), ('island', String), ('bill_length_mm', Float32), ('bill_depth_mm', Float32), ('flipper_length_mm', Int64), ('body_mass_g', Int64), ('sex', String), ('year', Int16)]) ``` ::: ::: ### Decimal: exact arithmetic {#sec-dm-decimal} Floats are binary fractions, so `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`. `Decimal` stores base-10 digits with a fixed scale, so values add up exactly. R has no built-in equivalent. ::: {#738f1833 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} prices = pl.Series(["0.10", "0.20"]) prices.cast(pl.Float64).sum(), prices.cast(pl.Decimal(10, 2)).sum() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` (0.30000000000000004, Decimal('0.30')) ``` ::: ::: Use it for money and for anything that has to add up exactly. ### The schema is an object {#sec-dm-schema} `df.schema` is a `pl.Schema`, an ordered mapping from column name to dtype, like `vapply(df, class, "")` but a real object you can pass around: ::: {#ba363efe .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_schema = penguins_df.schema penguins_schema.names()[:3], penguins_schema.dtypes()[:3], penguins_schema["year"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` (['species', 'island', 'bill_length_mm'], [String, String, Float64], Int64) ``` ::: ::: The same mapping works as an input: `pl.DataFrame(data, schema=...)`, `pl.read_csv(..., schema_overrides=...)`, `df.cast(...)`, and `df.match_to_schema(...)` (@sec-dm-recipes). ## Where it bites {#sec-dm-gotchas} | R behaviour | Polars behaviour | |---|---| | `c(1L, 2.5)` coerces to double | `pl.Series([1, 2.5])` raises; pass `dtype=` or `strict=False` | | `bind_rows()` coerces integer + double | `pl.concat()` raises; use `how="vertical_relaxed"` | | `as.integer("x")` → `NA` with a warning | `cast()` raises; `strict=False` gives null without a warning | | integer overflow → `NA` with a warning | integer arithmetic **wraps silently** | | counts (`n()`) are signed integers | counts and ranks are `UInt32` and wrap below zero | | integers are 32-bit | the default integer is `Int64` | : The differences at a glance {.striped} ### Integer arithmetic wraps silently {#sec-dm-overflow} ::: {#007efec0 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.select( int8_wrap=pl.lit(127, dtype=pl.Int8) + 1, int64_wrap=pl.lit(2**63 - 1, dtype=pl.Int64) + 1, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ```{=html}
shape: (1, 2)
int8_wrapint64_wrap
i8i64
-128-9223372036854775808
``` ::: ::: R would return `NA` and warn. Polars returns a wrong number, with no warning. In practice this happens after you shrink dtypes to save memory. Shrink `flights` (@sec-dm-recipes) and `dep_delay` becomes `Int16`, which holds values up to 32,767: ::: {#0def520d .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} int_cols = flights_df.select(cs.integer()).columns flights_df_small = flights_df.with_columns(flights_df[c].shrink_dtype() for c in int_cols) flights_df_small.filter(pl.col("dep_delay") == pl.col("dep_delay").max()).select( "dep_delay", delay_x100=pl.col("dep_delay") * 100, # Int16: 130,100 wraps delay_x100_ok=pl.col("dep_delay").cast(pl.Int64) * 100, # widen first ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ```{=html}
shape: (1, 3)
dep_delaydelay_x100delay_x100_ok
i16i16i64
1301-972130100
``` ::: ::: Aggregations are protected: `sum()` of a narrow integer column returns `Int64`. Element-wise arithmetic is not. **Rule:** keep narrow dtypes for storage, and widen before arithmetic that can grow values. ### Counts are unsigned {#sec-dm-unsigned} `pl.len()`, `.count()`, `.n_unique()`, `.null_count()`, `.arg_*()`, `with_row_index()`, and `rank()` with the `"min"`, `"max"`, `"dense"` or `"ordinal"` methods all return `UInt32`. Subtracting past zero wraps around to about 4.3 billion: ::: {#b266335b .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.group_by("species", maintain_order=True).agg( n=pl.len(), n_minus_100=pl.len() - 100, # Chinstrap: 68 − 100 → 4294967264 n_minus_100_ok=pl.len().cast(pl.Int64) - 100, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 4)
speciesnn_minus_100n_minus_100_ok
stru32u32i64
"Adelie"1525252
"Gentoo"1242424
"Chinstrap"684294967264-32
``` ::: ::: `rank()` with the default `"average"` method returns `Float64`, so it is safe. ### Hand-built frames don't coerce {#sec-dm-construction} Mixed Python values do not coerce, which bites when you type test data by hand: ::: {#0a7fa963 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.DataFrame({"dose": [1, 2.5]}) # R: tibble(dose = c(1L, 2.5)) → double ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
TypeError: unexpected value while building Series of type Int64; found value of type Float64: 2.5

This error occurred with the following context stack:
	[1] while constructing Series 'dose'


Hint: Try setting `strict=False` to allow passing data with mixed types.
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {#231732be .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.DataFrame({"dose": [1, 2.5]}, schema={"dose": pl.Float64}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 1)
dose
f64
1.0
2.5
``` ::: ::: (`[1.0, 2]` works, because the first value sets the dtype to `Float64` and `2` fits it.) Row-binding behaves the same way: ::: {#08b02a1f .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.concat([pl.DataFrame({"a": [1]}), pl.DataFrame({"a": [2.5]})]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
SchemaError: type Float64 is incompatible with expected type Int64

This error occurred with the following context stack:
	[1] failed to vstack column 'a'
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {#6de0367d .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.concat([pl.DataFrame({"a": [1]}), pl.DataFrame({"a": [2.5]})], how="vertical_relaxed") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 1)
a
f64
1.0
2.5
``` ::: ::: ## Recipes {#sec-dm-recipes} **Find the values that failed to parse** (≈ `readr::problems()`). Cast with `strict=False`, then keep the rows that were not null before but are null after: ::: {#cf336a78 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} doses_df_raw = pl.DataFrame({"dose_mg": ["10", "12.5", "n/a", "15", None, "2,5"]}) doses_df_parsed = doses_df_raw.with_columns( dose_num=pl.col("dose_mg").cast(pl.Float64, strict=False) ) doses_df_parsed.filter(pl.col("dose_mg").is_not_null() & pl.col("dose_num").is_null()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 2)
dose_mgdose_num
strf64
"n/a"null
"2,5"null
``` ::: ::: **Shrink a frame's memory.** `Series.shrink_dtype()` picks the narrowest integer width that fits each column (`Expr.shrink_dtype()` was removed in 2.0): ::: {#c154380a .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} { "flights_df (MB)": round(flights_df.estimated_size("mb"), 1), "flights_df_small (MB)": round(flights_df_small.estimated_size("mb"), 1), } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ``` {'flights_df (MB)': 43.2, 'flights_df_small (MB)': 15.0} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#c0aa6911 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df_small.select(cs.integer()).schema ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ``` Schema([('year', Int16), ('month', Int8), ('day', Int8), ('dep_time', Int16), ('sched_dep_time', Int16), ('dep_delay', Int16), ('arr_time', Int16), ('sched_arr_time', Int16), ('arr_delay', Int16), ('flight', Int16), ('air_time', Int16), ('distance', Int16), ('hour', Int8), ('minute', Int8)]) ``` ::: ::: Then watch for overflow when you compute on the result (@sec-dm-overflow). **Check a schema at the boundary** (≈ `pointblank::col_schema_match()`). `match_to_schema()` reorders columns to match the target and raises if a column is missing, extra, or has the wrong dtype. It is marked **unstable** in 2.0. ::: {#f0cfa089 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_expected = pl.Schema({**penguins_df.schema, "year": pl.String}) penguins_df.match_to_schema(penguins_expected) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
SchemaError: data type mismatch for column year: incoming: Int64 != target: String
``` ::: ::: ::: Options such as `extra_columns="ignore"` and `integer_cast="upcast"` relax individual rules. ## See also {#sec-dm-see-also} - Cheatsheet: [Import, Export & Inspect](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-io) · [Create & Modify Columns](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-mutate) (type conversion) - Next: [Expressions & Contexts](expressions.qmd) · [Missing Values](../types/missing.qmd) (null vs `NaN`) · [Lazy API](../scale/lazy.qmd) - Polars user guide: [Data types and structures](https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/concepts/data-types-and-structures/) · [Casting](https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/expressions/casting/) - Python API: [Data types](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/datatypes.html) · [`match_to_schema`](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/dataframe/api/polars.DataFrame.match_to_schema.html) - R side: *Advanced R*, [Vectors](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/vectors-chap.html) and [Names and values](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/names-values.html) (copy-on-modify)
